title: Rites of Passage and the Threshold Between Statuses
text:
Every society marks the moments when a person changes status, and it marks them with ceremony rather than with an announcement. Birth, adulthood, marriage and death are handled this way almost everywhere. Arnold van Gennep, writing a century ago, noticed that such ceremonies share a structure wherever they are found, and he named it the rite of passage.

He described three phases. The first is separation, in which the person is detached from the old role, often physically removed and stripped of ordinary clothing, name or company. The second is transition, during which they belong to neither the status they have left nor the one they are entering. The third is incorporation, when they are returned to the community and publicly received in the new position. Victor Turner concentrated on the middle phase and called it liminality, from the Latin word for a threshold. People in it are treated as ambiguous: ordinary rules of rank may be suspended, and initiates who undergo the same ordeal together often form an intense equality among themselves, which Turner named communitas. The analytical value is comparison. A graduation, a military induction and an initiation described by ethnographers share a form without sharing a meaning. The structure travels; the content belongs to each society.
points: Societies mark changes of status such as adulthood, marriage and death with ceremony, which van Gennep called rites of passage.
The first phase is separation, detaching the person from the old role, often physically.
The second is transition, when the person belongs to neither the old status nor the new.
The third is incorporation, the public return to the community in the new position.
Turner called the middle phase liminality, where rank is suspended and initiates form an equality he called communitas.
The value of the model is comparison: ceremonies share a structure while the meaning belongs to each society.
